Data and software
Use the dissertation project root as the working directory and begin with a fresh R session. The inspected project has no renv.lock, so the original package environment is not pinned. R and Quarto are required. Data processing uses packages including targets, tarchetypes, sf, tidyverse, readxl, DBI, and RSQLite; analyses and reports additionally use fixest, did, etwfe, marginaleffects, didFF, broom, modelsummary, gt, flextable, DT, and knitr. Check each source file’s imports and record sessionInfo() for a reproducibility run.
The inputs combine Cook County sales and parcels, FEMA flood boundaries and map timing, Microsoft building footprints, and First Street Flood Factor information. The current targets configuration selects data/raw/Assessor_-_Parcel_Sales_20260308.csv. The residential-PIN acquisition script uses a separately located PTAXSIM database; targets also reads a municipality lookup outside this repository. Manual GIS buffers, corrections, and parcel exclusions are additional inputs. Exact acquisition dates, permitted redistribution, and a complete input manifest remain to be documented; local availability is not the same as public availability. See the background source notes.


Computational workflow
External source data + manual GIS/lookup inputs
  -> _targets.R + R/ helpers
  -> processed spatial and sales exports
  -> analysis preparation / Q1 Quarto models / Q2 numbered scripts
  -> saved model, contrast, table, and diagnostic objects
  -> selected Quarto pages
  -> docs/ HTML
  -> separate publication step

Inventory inputs and versions. Preserve the dissertation snapshots and identify which saved output belongs to which source vintage. Do not replace a df_prep_* input with allsales_* solely because its name is newer.
Inspect the data pipeline. From the root, targets::tar_manifest() lists declared targets and targets::tar_outdated() identifies recorded changes. A later targets::tar_make() rebuilds affected targets after input paths are resolved. Some files are read inside commands rather than declared as file targets; these require explicit attention when inputs change.
Prepare analysis inputs. The current pipeline exports allsales_*; downstream models still require saved df_prep_* inputs. Restoring the reproducible bridge between these is a prerequisite for a clean build.
Generate analysis results. Q1 models are distributed across Quarto files. Q1_Model_Comparison.qmd writes the TWFE grid; etwfe_combined_mega_grid.qmd assembles the ETWFE grid from saved results. For Q2, the intended order in scripts/q2_dissertation_scripts/ is 00 preparation, 01 basic TWFE, 02 ETWFE, 03 main marginal effects, and 04 robustness. The Flood Factor form-check sequence is 00, 01, 02, with 03 a loading example. The numbered script source paths have been repaired; verify the saved model version and external inputs before running these sequences.
Prepare diagnostics. Existing Q2 plot and model RDS files are under outputs/q2_assumption_tests/. Their runner now reuses the existing prepared dataset or calls the existing Flood Factor preparation script when the dataset is absent. The website can display saved objects, but a clean diagnostic rebuild is not yet documented end to end. Historical distributional-test scripts contain exploratory alternatives; do not run them indiscriminately, because some overwrite outputs.
Render and inspect. The website explicitly renders selected pages to docs/. For a chosen page, use quarto render filename.qmd; use quarto render for the configured site. Some pages fit models during rendering. The freeze: auto setting can reuse cached execution in project builds, so external RDS changes must be considered when refreshing output. Inspect tables, labels, links, and figure provenance before publication.
Publish separately. Confirm the approved local sources and outputs are versioned and publish through the project’s chosen GitHub Pages workflow. Preserve the stable homepage URL used by the dissertation. This documentation edit does not publish the site.

The following models separate the timing of Flood Factor information release from the underlying level of flood risk. Property fixed effects absorb time-invariant parcel characteristics, while year fixed effects control for broader market conditions.
event == TRUE for all sales that occurred after First Street released its flood risk data.
high_ff_score == TRUE for properties that had a Flood Factor score of 5 or higher.


The binary specifications estimate whether properties with high Flood Factor scores experienced differential price changes after Flood Factor information became publicly available. The specification using i(event, high_ff_score, ref = FALSE) keeps the identified post-release contrast while avoiding the time-invariant main effect that is absorbed by property fixed effects.

title: Q1 Nearby Property Controls
text:
Reading the model tables
The outcome is the logarithm of sale price. The models include property (pin) fixed effects and cluster standard errors at the 10-digit parcel (pin10) level. The geographic time controls vary by section. Preliminary and effective map designations are estimated separately; within each section, the preliminary-map table precedes the effective-map table.
In the tables labeled I and II, I estimates the added-to-SFHA indicator and II estimates the removed-from-SFHA indicator. The corresponding Subset columns exclude the opposite transition and the always-SFHA group (for additions) or never-SFHA group (for removals). Where shown, Symmetric uses the in-SFHA indicator, while column 0 includes addition and removal indicators together. Positive coefficients indicate higher estimated sale prices and negative coefficients indicate lower estimated prices; a log coefficient b converts to a percentage change as 100 * (exp(b) - 1). Stars and standard errors should be read alongside the sample and fixed-effects specification.
These tables use the existing prepared dataset outputs/q2_marginaleffects/bldg_sfha_q2_dissertation_prepped.RDS; despite its folder name, the models below use Q1 FEMA map-transition indicators. The 300-meter indicator comes from data/processed/bldgswithin300mof_SFHA_arcgis.xlsx, matched on PIN10. This page documents the implemented samples. It does not establish that the current tables reproduce the exact 15.9% and 18.1% estimates reported in the dissertation; that requires a separate check of the original data vintage, model, and coefficient transformation.

section: Dissertation page 2: coverage calculation and provenance
text:
Dissertation page 2: coverage calculation and provenance
Page 2 compares the residential share in FEMA SFHAs with the share assigned major flood risk by First Street. The existing calculation below counts class-200 records with Flood Factor scores of at least 5 and divides by the number of distinct (pin, class) records in the 2023 residential file. It is a population calculation, not a share of sales or of the Q1 regression sample. Missing Flood Factor scores do not enter the numerator but remain in the denominator.
scripts/pull_distinct_resPINs.R identifies the residential file as a PTAXSIM extraction covering 2006-2023, using the local ptaxsim-2023.0.0.db database. scripts/pull_floodfactor_pin_list.R identifies the scores as a 2019 Flood Factor snapshot retrieved through the Cook County Assessor parcel API (nj4t-kc8j) and writes the processed score file after duplicate handling. Those script descriptions establish the intended sources; they do not independently verify the vintage of every current CSV or record its actual download date.

make_control_groups <- function(df, 
                                ever_added,
                                ever_removed,
                    pre_eff_change_type, 
                    type = c("pre", "eff")
                                ){
  
  # Treated Group A: Added to Risk Zone
  group_T_A <- df |>
    filter( {{ever_added}} == TRUE )
  
  # Treated Group B: Removed from Risk Zone
  group_T_B <- df |> 
      filter( {{ever_removed}}  == TRUE)

  # Control Group A:  Never in SFHA, FIRM panels never updated
    
   if(type == "pre"){
   group_C_A <- df |> 
      filter(
        {{pre_eff_change_type}} == "Never SFHA" &
             pre_date_chr %in% c("2005-01-01")
         )
  }else if(type == "eff"){  # for effective maps
  group_C_A <- df |> 
      filter(
        {{pre_eff_change_type}} == "Never SFHA" &
         eff_date_chr %in% c("2008-08-19") 
         ) 
  }  

    # Control Group B: Never in SFHA, FIRM Panels are updated
    group_C_B  <- df |> 
      filter( 
        {{pre_eff_change_type}} == "Never SFHA" &
         (eff_date_chr %in% c("2019-11-01", "2021-09-10") | 
             pre_date_chr %in% c("2015-02-12", "2019-07-01", "2021-09-22")
         )
         )

    # Control Group C: Always in SFHA, FIRM Panels are not updated 
    if(type == "pre"){
    group_C_C <- df |> 
      filter(
        {{pre_eff_change_type}} == "Always SFHA" &             
          pre_date_chr %in% c("2005-01-01")
      )}
    else if(type == "eff") {  # this probably is tainted by prelim map cohort in 2021 though....
    group_C_C <- df |> 
      filter(
        {{pre_eff_change_type}} == "Always SFHA" &
         (eff_date_chr %in% c("2008-08-19") )
      )
    
    group_C_C_alt <- df |> 
      filter(
        {{pre_eff_change_type}} == "Always SFHA" &
         (eff_date_chr %in% c("2008-08-19") | 
            pre_date_chr %in% c("2005-01-01")
          )
      )
    }
    
    # Always in SFHA but FIRM panels have been recently updated
   
    if(type == "eff") {
      group_C_D <- df |> 
        filter(
        {{pre_eff_change_type}} == "Always SFHA" &
         (eff_date_chr %in% c("2019-11-01", "2021-09-10"))
         )
      
       group_C_D_alt <- df |> 
        filter(
        {{pre_eff_change_type}} == "Always SFHA" &
         (eff_date_chr %in% c("2019-11-01", "2021-09-10") | 
             pre_date_chr %in% c("2015-02-12", "2019-07-01", "2021-09-22")
             )
         )
    } else if (type == "pre") {
      group_C_D <- df |> 
         filter(
        {{pre_eff_change_type}} == "Always SFHA" &
             pre_date_chr %in% c("2015-02-12", "2019-07-01", "2021-09-22")
         )
    }
      list(
    group_T_A = group_T_A,
    group_T_B = group_T_B,
    group_C_A = group_C_A,
    group_C_B = group_C_B,
    group_C_C = group_C_C,
    group_C_D = group_C_D

  )

}

The small number of treated properties discussed around dissertation page 56 can vary sharply with the exposure definition. This inventory uses the four current df_prep_*_v2026_03 exports and the project’s manual parcel exclusions. It counts post-transition sales and distinct 10-digit parcels separately for preliminary/effective additions/removals. These are input-sample counts, not the effective estimation sample of every model in the saved grids: missing variables, fixed-effect singleton removal, control-group restrictions, and geographic exclusions can change a fitted model’s sample. They should not be labeled as exact dissertation table counts until reconciled with the original fitted models.

  `Building - SFHA` = "data/processed/targets/sales/df_prep_bldg_v2026_03.RDS",
  `Parcel - SFHA` = "data/processed/targets/sales/df_prep_land_v2026_03.RDS",
  `Building - 1-in-500` = "data/processed/targets/sales/df_prep_risk500_v2026_03.RDS",

q1_exposure_counts <- purrr::imap_dfr(q1_exposure_paths, function(path, definition) {
  if (!file.exists(path)) stop("Missing exposure dataset: ", path)
  d <- readRDS(path) |>
    dplyr::filter(!pin10 %in% drop_parcels | (pin10 == "0113301013" & sale_year > 2014))
  indicators <- c(
    `Preliminary: added` = "addedto_prelim_sfha",
    `Preliminary: removed` = "removedfrom_prelim_sfha",
    `Effective: added` = "addedto_eff_sfha",
    `Effective: removed` = "removedfrom_eff_sfha"
  )
  if (!all(c("pin10", unname(indicators)) %in% names(d))) {
    stop("Missing transition identifiers in ", path)
  }
  purrr::imap_dfr(indicators, function(variable, transition) {
    flag <- as.character(d[[variable]])
    if (!all(stats::na.omit(flag) %in% c("TRUE", "FALSE", "1", "0"))) {
      stop("Unexpected transition coding in ", path, ": ", variable)
    }
    treated <- !is.na(flag) & flag %in% c("TRUE", "1")
    tibble::tibble(
      Definition = definition, Transition = transition,
      `Input sales` = nrow(d), `Treated sales` = sum(treated),
      `Treated parcels` = dplyr::n_distinct(d$pin10[treated], na.rm = TRUE),
      `Missing transition flag` = sum(is.na(flag))
    )
  })
})

Additions: event study and pretrend tests
Properties added to the preliminary SFHA are compared with never-SFHA properties. Event time is relative to the preliminary map year; sales earlier than the preliminary date within that year are assigned to year -1. The endpoint bins pool years at or below -5 and at or above +5. Year -1 is the omitted reference period.
The plotted model uses logged sale price, property and year fixed effects, and standard errors clustered by 10-digit parcel. The coefficient table below the plot lists estimated pretreatment leads; the Wald test jointly tests the included leads -5 through -2 against zero relative to year -1. Rejection raises concerns about the specification or pre-event comparability. Non-rejection is not proof of parallel trends, especially when treated samples are small.

title: Q1 Figures and Tables
text:
Two-year-early placebo tests
Appendix A discusses whether estimated changes appear before the preliminary map date. These placebo models move each preliminary date two years earlier, restrict observations to sales strictly before the actual preliminary date, and estimate the treated-by-placebo-period interaction with property and year fixed effects and parcel-clustered standard errors. Removals are displayed first, then additions.
A nonzero placebo estimate can reflect anticipation, differential trends, or other misspecification; it does not identify which explanation is responsible. A non-significant estimate does not rule these out. The final two tables use the actual preliminary date and the broader time window, providing a reference specification rather than additional placebo tests.


Code
# df_prep must have: pin, pin10, sale_date, sale_year, pre_date, prelim_sfha_category, log_price

run_placebo_did <- function(df,
                            fake_shift_years = 2,
                            treated_label = "Added to prelim SFHA",
                            unit_fe = "pin",
                            time_fe = "sale_year",
                            cluster_var = "pin10") {
  if(treated_label == "Added to prelim SFHA"){
    df <- df |> filter(prelim_sfha_category %in% c("Added to prelim SFHA", "Never SFHA"))
  }
  if(treated_label == "Removed from prelim SFHA"){
    df <- df |> filter(prelim_sfha_category %in% c("Removed from prelim SFHA", "Always SFHA"))
  }
  df_placebo <- df |>
    mutate(
      treated = prelim_sfha_category == treated_label,
      placebo_date = pre_date %m-% years(fake_shift_years),
      placebo_post = sale_date >= placebo_date
    ) |>
    # keep only observations strictly before the *real* event (so placebo is truly placebo)
    filter(sale_date < pre_date) |>
    # optional: keep only observations with a defined placebo_date
    filter(!is.na(placebo_date))

  fml <- as.formula(paste0(
    "log_price ~ treated * placebo_post | ",
    unit_fe, " + ", time_fe
  ))

  feols(
    fml,
    cluster = as.formula(paste0("~", cluster_var)),
    data = df_placebo
  )
}

section: Regional controls and conditional parallel trends
text:
Regional controls and conditional parallel trends
Appendix A considers whether regional housing-market differences affect the Q1 comparisons. The specifications below adapt the existing triad-by-year event studies in q1_assumption_tests.qmd to the same addition and removal samples used above. They replace common year effects with sale_year^Triad while retaining property fixed effects and parcel-clustered standard errors. These are region-by-year fixed effects, not separate linear trend slopes.
The comparisons use a common complete-case sample for each treatment direction, so differences between the two specifications are not caused by missing triad identifiers. The joint tests concern the included pretreatment coefficients relative to year -1; failure to reject does not establish the unobserved post-treatment counterfactual. These tables are newly assembled from the existing specifications, not a verified reproduction of a numbered dissertation table.


Code
q1_regional_samples <- list(
  Added = df_es_add,
  Removed = df_es_removed
)
q1_regional_models <- lapply(q1_regional_samples, function(d) {
  d <- d |>
    dplyr::filter(is.finite(sale_price), sale_price > 0) |>
    tidyr::drop_na(pin, pin10, sale_year, Triad, event_time_binned, treated)
  list(
    `Common year effects` = fixest::feols(
      log(sale_price) ~ i(event_time_binned, treated, ref = -1) | pin + sale_year,
      cluster = ~pin10, data = d
    ),
    `Triad-by-year effects` = fixest::feols(
      log(sale_price) ~ i(event_time_binned, treated, ref = -1) | pin + sale_year^Triad,
      cluster = ~pin10, data = d
    )
  )
})
for (direction in names(q1_regional_models)) {
  cat("\n", direction, "to/from preliminary SFHA: coefficient comparison\n")
  print(fixest::etable(q1_regional_models[[direction]], signif.code = c("***" = .001, "**" = .01, "*" = .05, "+" = .10),
                      keep = "%event_time_binned::"))
  for (specification in names(q1_regional_models[[direction]])) {
    cat("\nJoint pretreatment test:", direction, "-", specification, "\n")
    print(fixest::wald(q1_regional_models[[direction]][[specification]],
                      keep = "event_time_binned::-(5|4|3|2)"))
  }
  fixest::iplot(q1_regional_models[[direction]][["Triad-by-year effects"]],
                xlab = "Years relative to preliminary map year",
                main = paste(direction, "- triad-by-year fixed effects"))
}

text:
Outcome transformations
Appendix A (printed pages 95-97) discusses sale price in levels, logarithms, inverse price, and inverse hyperbolic sine. The plots below assemble all four transformations for the Q1 event-study samples. They use the same observations across transformations: finite, strictly positive prices in the pretreatment period, with addition and removal comparisons shown separately. The last two plots are supporting variations, not estimates of a new treatment effect.
Points are means of transformed sale prices by calendar year and treatment group, not transformations of the group mean. The panels use separate vertical scales. A year can pool observations from different preliminary-map cohorts, and the mix of sold properties can change over time; these descriptive plots therefore supplement the event studies rather than proving parallel trends. Inverse price is decreasing in price, so its direction must be interpreted accordingly. This newly assembled comparison is not an exact reconstruction of dissertation Figures 15-16.


Code
q1_transformation_data <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  Added = df_es_add,
  Removed = df_es_removed,
  .id = "comparison"
) |>
  dplyr::filter(sale_date < pre_date, is.finite(sale_price), sale_price > 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    group = dplyr::if_else(treated, "Transition group", "Comparison group"),
    `Sale price` = sale_price,
    `Log sale price` = log(sale_price),
    `Inverse sale price` = 1 / sale_price,

Saved distributional parallel-trends diagnostics
Appendix A (printed pages 98-99) reports distributional diagnostics associated with Roth and Sant’Anna’s functional-form analysis. Existing results were located in scripts/Q1_SFHA_DiD_test.R and its saved didFF objects. The cells below display those saved results without re-estimating them or running the exploratory script.
The unlogged 2014/2022 object has a saved p-value of 0.99778, consistent with the rounded 0.998 in the dissertation. A second unlogged object has p-value 1. The saved logged-price object has p-value 0. These are different historical specifications; they should not be presented as uniformly supporting the same conclusion. The script overwrites the logged-price output during its later exploratory specification, so it is not a clean same-sample levels-versus-logs comparison. A large p-value is a failure to reject the diagnostic’s null, not proof of parallel trends or of the causal interpretation.

didFF_Q1_model_notlogged.rds
Uses the older parcel dataset df_prep_land_updated_final.rds, retains 2014 and 2022 sales, averages within property-year, and assigns the transition group to 2022. Outcome: sale price.


didFF_Q1_model_out.rds

didFF_model_Q1_out2.rds

title: Q2 Figures and Tables
text:
From coefficients to subgroup contrasts
For a linear log-price model, let x(post, h, s, r) be the model row for post-release status, high-score status, SFHA group, and region. The post-versus-pre contrast for a subgroup is [x(1,h,s,r) - x(0,h,s,r)]' beta. The high-versus-low difference in that post/pre contrast subtracts the same expression evaluated at h = 0 from the expression at h = 1. These are different estimands: a post/pre change for high-risk properties is not automatically the high-minus-low difference-in-differences effect.
For a contrast vector c, its standard error uses the full covariance matrix, sqrt(c' V c), including covariances among interaction coefficients. The existing analysis computes contrasts with marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(). Saved estimates are in log points unless explicitly transformed; 100 * (exp(estimate) - 1) gives the corresponding percentage conversion, not estimate itself. Nonlinear transformation and averaging should not be interchanged without specifying the target estimand.
The existing marginal-effect sections display the saved contrasts. Their nearby code records each call’s variables, by, and any newdata grid. These details determine the comparison and weighting and should be retained when linking a dissertation table to its underlying model.

text:
Placebo analysis: existing 2017 cutoff
Dissertation Appendix B, Table XXV (p. 106), prints 659,942 observations for the actual event. We treat that count as a reporting error. The corresponding model with SFHA interactions uses 666,566 observations on the saved dissertation data, consistent with the sample size in the main text. Its high Flood Factor × post coefficient rounds to the printed −0.103.
Use each model’s actual estimation sample. The search for the origin of 659,942 is closed. If a future dissertation model independently yields exactly 659,942 estimation observations, flag it as a possible source of the printed count and record its specification and input file. A count match alone leaves the provenance uncertain.
The first two models restrict sales to 2019 or earlier and define post-placebo as sale_year > 2017: 2018-2019 versus earlier years. The next two show actual-release specifications using the broader prepared sample. Their time windows and some fixed effects differ, so they are reference models rather than an exact one-variable timing substitution. This makes the existing implementation explicit without silently changing the dissertation’s placebo design.

Distributional diagnostics and anticipation
The saved distributional diagnostics come from scripts/Q2_FloodFactor_didFF_test.R. That script uses the older data/processed/df_prep_buildings.rds input, applies its missing-data and parcel filters, averages observations within property-year, and assigns the treated group to 2020 for a property with a high Flood Factor score and an observed post-release sale. The last condition makes group assignment depend on observed sales as well as risk status. This historical construction must be reviewed before treating these outputs as a definitive check of the current main model.
The logged and unlogged saved objects both report p-values of 1. The displays below load those results without rerunning the exploratory script. They are not evidence that the current main-model sample passes every identifying assumption: failure to reject a distributional diagnostic does not prove mean parallel trends, absence of anticipation, or causal identification.

What the anticipation checks can establish
The pre-event slope tests and the pre-2020 placebo sample address patterns before the recorded Flood Factor release. The existing placebo code defines its post period as years greater than 2017, so 2018-2019 are post-placebo and 2017 itself remains pre-placebo. A significant placebo interaction may reflect differential trends, other events, or anticipation; it does not distinguish among them. A non-significant result cannot rule out advance information or limited power. The assumed information date and sample construction must be considered alongside these diagnostics.

Create a long-format dataset with:
PIN | year | in_sfha | flood_factor_score | in_lomr | av | sale_price | sold | treatment | post
Key Variables:

year: Matching the time of assessment or sale
in_sfha: 0/1 for floodplain presence that year
flood_factor_score: Ordinal flood risk score (e.g., 1–10)
in_lomr: 0/1 if parcel is in a LOMR revision area that year
av: Assessed value that year
sale_price: Sale price (if sold that year)
sold: 0/1 if there was a sale
treatment: 1 if the PIN was ever added to (or removed from) the SFHA (i.e., eligible for treatment)
post: 1 if observation is after the map change
added_to_sfha = (in_sfha_2024 == 1 & in_sfha_2018 == 0) removed_from_sfha = (in_sfha_2024 == 0 & in_sfha_2018 == 1)
treatment = 1 if added_to_sfha | removed_from_sfha

Key Variables:

year: Matching the time of assessment or sale

flood_factor_score: Ordinal flood risk score (e.g., 1–10)
in_lomr: 0/1 if parcel is in a LOMR revision area that year
av: Assessed value that year
sale_price: Sale price (if sold that year)
sold: 0/1 if there was a sale
treatment: 1 if the PIN was ever added to (or removed from) the SFHA (i.e., eligible for treatment)
post: 1 if observation is after the map change
added_to_sfha = (in_sfha_2024 == 1 & in_sfha_2018 == 0) removed_from_sfha = (in_sfha_2024 == 0 & in_sfha_2018 == 1)
treatment = 1 if added_to_sfha | removed_from_sfha
